data.title: Weight regain after diet pill use linked to rise in suicidal thoughts: Study
data.description:
(NewsNation) — People who used prescription weight loss medication and later regained the weight reported suicidal thoughts at more than four times the rate of people who never took the drugs, a new study found.

Researchers led by Dr. Son Ki-young, a family medicine professor at Asan Medical Center, analyzed data from 27,741 adults — 10,908 men and 16,833 women — who took part in a national health survey between 2013 and 2022.

Of those, 846 reported using prescription weight-loss drugs in the prior year, while 26,895 did not, according to the study published in Korean Journal of Family Practice.

Compared with people who hadn’t used the meds, those who had were 2.7 times more likely to report suicidal thoughts, 1.9 times more likely to report creating a plan and 1.7 times more likely to report an attempt.

They were also 1.9 times more likely to report depression lasting more than two weeks and twice as likely to have sought mental health counseling, the data shows.

The sharpest numbers came from a subgroup: people who took the medication and still gained weight.

Their odds of suicidal thoughts were 4.2 times higher than those who never used the drugs, while depression and counseling odds were roughly 1.9 and 1.8 times higher, the researchers found.

The study’s authors said the pattern likely reflects more than a direct drug effect.

“The increase in suicide-related index, among those who regained weight after weight-loss medication, is not just related to the neurological and psychiatric effects of the medicine itself,” the research team wrote, according to the International Business Times. “It is likely to be connected in a complex way to the psychological and social elements related to failing to control one’s weight.”

The study is observational, meaning it can’t prove the medications caused the mental health symptoms — only that a correlation exists.

The survey period also mostly predates widespread use of newer GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide (Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Zepbound, Mounjaro) in South Korea.

The sample instead largely reflects older appetite suppressants, including phentermine, diethylpropion, phendimetrazine, topiramate and orlistat — stimulant-based drugs already linked to anxiety, insomnia and mood changes.

People with severe obesity already have higher baseline rates of depression, anxiety and body-image distress and a one-time survey can’t separate preexisting symptoms from new ones.

In January, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) asked drugmakers to remove suicidal-ideation warning language from the labels of Saxenda, Wegovy and Zepbound after a review of 91 placebo-controlled trials involving more than 107,000 patients found no increased risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior tied to GLP-1 drugs.

Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly both said they support the FDA’s findings, though Lilly’s consumer materials still direct patients to watch for mood changes and contact a doctor if symptoms are “new, worse or worry you.”

data.title: Laura Ingraham presses Trump on $5,000 'bribe'
data.description:
Turns out, very few people were impressed by President Trump’s bribe attempt Wednesday night.  

If you missed it, here it is.

$5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win control of Congress. That estimated price tag is at least $1.3 trillion and would require congressional approval.  

One of the best critiques came from conservative National Review columnist Charles C.W. Cooke, who called Trump’s proposal “just preposterous.”  

He released an opinion piece saying: “Painfully aware that, once the midterms are over, he risks being gradually consigned to irrelevance, President Trump has hit once again upon a Hail Mary plan for political success. That plan is bribery.”  

He went on to say: “Last night, after vocally condemning the rise of socialism in the United States, Trump pledged some of his own.”  

The contradiction really is crazy. At the convention, Trump warned voters that Democrats are socialists who want to give away their money. Then he proposed giving Americans $5,000 each if Republicans win. For nothing else other than the fact that they won.  

If the policies are working, why is the sales pitch a check?  

The enhanced ACA premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025, increasing premiums for many Americans. Oil and gas prices have surged amid the ongoing Iran conflict, and tariffs remain a major part of the administration’s economic strategy while they hurt the average American consumer.  

So instead of explaining those policies and why Americans should stick with them, the message here seems to be: Here’s $5,000. Let me continue to make your life unaffordable.  

Even if you’re not upset about the fact that this sounded like a bribe, this is hardly the first promise of an erroneous payout that had absolutely no merit or chance of happening. CNN’s Manu Raju helped refresh our memory. 

The reality is, there is no $5,000 check getting approved by Congress, and federal law does prohibit offering payment for voting. So this is not happening.  

But between the tariffs, the Iran war and the mass deportation agenda that have all negatively affected our economy, this convention helped me realize that the Republican message is now: If you can’t beat ’em, bribe ’em. 

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

data.title: Juror says testimony by Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband influenced her
data.description:
(NewsNation) — A juror in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial claimed in a new interview that testimony from the Massachusetts mother’s ex-husband Patrick Clancy was “very impactful” in her decision to vote not guilty.

“I think the prosecution tried to nudge Patrick (Clancy) to say something derogatory, and he wouldn’t,” juror Paula Devlin told “CBS Mornings.”

“And that was very impactful, even after all this time and even after knowing this happened and losing his three children, he still couldn’t say anything really bad about her,” she added.

Clancy is still facing murder charges in the deaths of her three young children. A five-week trial ended in a mistrial last week, after the jury failed to come to a unanimous verdict.

The jury was split 11-1 in favor of finding her not guilty by reason of insanity, according to the jury foreperson, after her attorney argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and shouldn’t be held criminally responsible.

Dr. Resnick’s testimony also made an impact

Devlin also cited Dr. Phillip Resnick’s testimony on altruistic filicide as influencing her vote. Psychiatric News describes this condition as a situation where a mother believes “death to be in the child’s best interest.”

Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist and expert in filicide (the killing of a child by a parent), testified on behalf of the defense that Clancy murdered her children not out of malice, but because she was so deeply suicidal that her psychosis made her believe they couldn’t live without her. Prosecutors had argued that the murders were premeditated.

“All throughout the trial … there had been nothing but good said about Lindsay and how amazing of a mother she was, how much she loved her children,” Devlin explained. “And then to hear somebody talking about a real reason why all of a sudden this could happen, that was really impactful.”

Patrick Clancy’s lawyer threatens legal ‘consequences’

As the case has made headlines in recent months, videos have circulated on social media of people theorizing about Patrick Clancy’s potential culpability.

Some have focused on whether he gave his wife enough support, based on what he knew about the state of her mental health at the time. Others have gone as far as making unsubstantiated claims that the mother is innocent and that her husband was responsible for the deaths.

Amid the online speculation, the ex-husband’s attorney has threatened legal “consequences” over what he described to CBS News as a “relentless, escalating and destructive defamation campaign” surrounding his former wife’s murder trial.

NewsNation’s Steph Whiteside, Alicia Sitz and staff contributed to this report.

data.title: Lutnick says $5K dividend would not use taxpayer dollars
data.description:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Thursday that the $5,000 dividends President Trump promised U.S. adults earlier this week would not come from taxpayer money.

In an interview with NBC News at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, Lutnick said, “It’s not tax money.”

“Together we’re going to deliver that plan and we’re going to pay that money to the Americans, and not from taxpayer money,” Lutnick continued.

Trump announced the dividends on the GOP’s midterm convention but said the money would only be given if Republicans maintained control of both chambers in Congress. The proposal would disburse a total of $1.2 trillion in dividends to roughly 270 million U.S. adults. 

Lutnick said the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers.”

When asked where the money would come from, Lutnick cited the Trump Platinum Card – which is not launched yet – that would require immigration applicants to join a waitlist and allows for future applicants to live in the U.S. for 270 days per year without being subject to tax on non-U.S. income.

Applicants would have to pay a $15,000 processing fee, undergo Department of Homeland Security vetting and pay an additional $5 million contribution to the U.S. government to be guaranteed citizenship.

“We have a waitlist of more than 100,000 people who want to come,” Lutnick said. “That’s $500 billion dollars.”

He also mentioned the investment the federal government made into Intel last year as another source of possible funds which Trump said generated more than $30 billion over the last several months.

“Everybody knows we got just about 500 million shares, and the stock was $20, and now it’s $100, so we’re up $50 billion,” Lutnick stated. 

White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett has also suggested Friday the funds could come from a reconciliation package.

The proposal has divided figures within the GOP as Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) was critical of the proposal, noting the rising national debt as a major drawback to the proposal.

“What I don’t think you want to do is borrow another trillion-and-a-half dollars and then just try to flood that into the economy, because that will lead to more inflation,” DeSantis said.

data.title: Top Ukrainian official gives inside look at the war with Russia
data.description:
(NewsNation) EXCLUSIVE — Four and a half years after Russia attacked Ukraine, the war between the two countries continues to rage. But this is not just a regional war, according to Lt. Gen. Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.

Budanov says we could be at the beginning of World War III, if peace does not prevail soon. 

“North Korean troops are in Europe. Russia is supporting Iran that fights the U.S. and civilized countries of the Gulf. There’s a whole range of hostilities happening in various countries of Africa where you see the same players support one or the other side,” the official told NewsNation.

Despite multiple conflicts around the world, his focus is on Ukraine and finding an end to the more than four-year-long war.

In an exclusive, far-reaching interview with NewsNation, Budanov — effectively the chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelensky and the former head of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency — paints a clear-eyed picture of the war, the importance of the relationship with the U.S., Ukraine’s stability after a period of internal strife and what he personally relies on to navigate life during wartime.

The interview was conducted prior to the U.S. delegation traveling to Ukraine, but after CIA Director John Ratcliffe reportedly visited Moscow.

Of the official’s trip to the Russian capital, Budanov says he views it as a “positive thing because you need to always be talking.”

He added he was glad Ratcliffe spoke with the Russians about a trilateral summit, because it shows that the U.S. is ready for it. Ukraine, he continued, is also ready but he does not believe Russia is.

This past weekend’s trips, by special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, to Russia and Ukraine to jumpstart talks is a step forward, though nothing concrete has come of it yet.

A Ukrainian source familiar with the discussions in Kyiv, said they “were productive, some new ideas were discussed, and the goal is to end the war by the winter.” 

If the war ends

FILE – Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Kyrylo Budanov speaks during press conference in Kyiv, Ukraine, Feb. 23, 2025. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka, File)

Budanov said he would “love this war to end in a just way so the aggressor would be punished.”

He also acknowledged that whenever a ceasefire is declared, the territorial lines will be “formed by the real state of affairs, the real status quo on the front line.”

So, it’s possible Ukraine could lose some territory given Russia currently occupies sections of the Donbas region. He expects the end to fighting to come with the help and mediation of the U.S., and specifically Trump.

In the meantime, the war is at a stalemate, the lieutenant general noted, adding, “Russia is not getting any strategic advances on the battlefield.”

He explained that Moscow may get “certain tactical gains, but we are getting certain tactical gains, too.”

“That is the reason why Russia switched to ordinary tactics of drone and missile terror against civilian populations and against civilian infrastructure,” Budanov continued.

Wednesday, a Russian drone struck near a mall killing at least two and wounding 14 others. Another strike hit a residential apartment building in Kyiv killing one person and injuring seven, including two children. There have been regular fatal attacks against civilians by Russia.

When asked if Ukraine would change tactics and target civilians as well, Budanov says, “we are not terrorists. And we’re only targeting legitimate military targets.”

Ukraine has focused their attacks on oil refineries, factories and warehouses, adding an economic strain to the attacks.

Zelensky said Ukrainian forces on Wednesday struck targets including a naval base and terminal for loading oil, as well as military port facilities and warships carrying missiles in Russia’s Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk and in the Krasnodar region.

Civilian deaths

Firefighters put out a fire after a Russian drone hit a gas station in Kyiv, Ukraine, Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)

A United Nations report shows the agency verified at least 16,000 Ukrainian civilian deaths between the start of the war on Feb. 24, 2022 through July 2026.

That number likely doesn’t reflect all deaths, with unconfirmed deaths reported and incomplete information from some areas. Since the July report, the number has increased. 

Available data shows far more Ukrainian citizens are dying than Russian citizens.

According to The New York Times, which cites the tracking group Conflict Intelligence Team, in the first seven months of this year, 327 civilians died in Russia from attacks. In Ukraine, the number was 1,695 civilians. 

Patriot missile systems

FILE – Ukrainian Air Force’s F-16 fighter jets fly over a Patriot Air and Missile Defense System in an undisclosed location in Ukraine, on Aug. 4, 2024. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky, File)

Budanov explained that one challenge for Ukraine is defending itself against Russia’s use of ballistic missiles, which are harder to intercept without a Patriot missile system.

Ukraine has asked the Trump administration for more missiles, and there has been talk of U.S. defense companies licensing the technology. 

The official told NewsNation, “I’m not saying give that to us as a gift. I’m saying sell to us.”

“It is the civilian population who die because of those Russian ballistic missiles and Russian drones … We need those interceptor missiles to protect our women and children, to protect the future of this country,” he added.

Concerns about mobilization

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky looks on during his meeting with President Trump on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026.

Ukraine’s leaders are aware that Russia may be preparing a large mobilization, which likely includes drafting more Russians to fight. The Kyiv Post reports Russia is preparing to send up to 400,000 troops to the front in large part to take the Donbas, a region of Ukraine that Russia is contesting.

“I can say that nothing good comes out of it for Ukraine, but I can also say that for Russia, it will only end with a huge increase in [the] number of dead bodies,” Budanov said in the interview. ” It will be another challenge for our defense industry here in Ukraine.”

He continued, “Because we’ll have to significantly increase the production of drones that are used to kill the enemy and also projectiles and shells of various types. Because we need to be saving our soldiers.”

Should Ukraine need to mobilize further, the general says, “there is, of course, a degree of tiredness among the population, but still, thank God, the population understands that a collapse at the front line means a collapse of statehood.”

Working in Russia’s favor is their large population, something Budanov acknowledges. According to Worldometer, there are about 143 million people in Russia to Ukraine’s 40 million. With so many people, Moscow can afford to lose more and replace them quickly on the battlefield.

Ratcliffe has said the life expectancy of a Russian soldier at the front lines is just 30 minutes. More often than not, they’re killed by a drone. 

The general noted that Ukraine’s technological adaptation has kept them in the fight and started to turn the tide of the war. He added that technologically well-equipped personnel can repel attacks of a larger enemy force.

Ukraine has arguably become the best in the world at drone warfare. Zelensky hopes the country will produce up to 10 million this year.

Budanov said the future will include more automation, more reliance on cyber systems, further integration of AI and more automated weapons systems. 

“But still, the role of a human soldier at the battlefield, it will stay and it will remain,” he added.

Sanctions and the dueling bills

While the U.S. has issued sanctions against Russia, a new bill that passed the Senate would be far more punitive in the hopes of pushing Russia to the negotiating table and ending the war. 

Originally ushered by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), the bill would, in part, allow the president to impose economic pressure via a tariff of up to 100 percent on all goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, as well as countries helping Russia evade oil sanctions.

“We have high hopes for this bill. And to my personal opinion, this very bill is a large advantage to the U.S. and the presidency in particular,” Budanov says.

He believes it would provide leverage to the institution of the presidency, and in this case, Trump could add or remove tariffs depending on whether Russia’s President Vladimir Putin listens to him.

It is exactly that power that has some Democratic House leaders concerned. Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, explained that he and other Democrats support Ukraine and want to punish Russia, but believe their bill is more effective because it would mandate the sanctions, Trump couldn’t waive them and it would address humanitarian aid as well as munitions support. 

Perhaps most importantly to Meeks, he pointed to the institution of Congress while telling NewsNation they are the ones “that deal with tariffs.”

“That’s what the Constitution says…we should not be giving that authority away to any president, Democrat or Republican,” the New York lawmaker added.

Meeks said he’s open to a conversation with Zelensky and would even travel to Ukraine for it. With the midterm elections around the corner, it is unlikely the current bill will advance past the House floor, leaving the issue of harsher sanctions against Russia unresolved.  

Ukraine’s internal strife

FILE – Ukraine’s former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov speaks to journalists during a joint press conference with Sweden’s Defense Minister Pal Jonson in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, July 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky, file)

In mid-July, Zelensky fired then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov in a move that was seen as favoring top military commander General Oleksandr Syrski, who was considered more “old-school” in terms of his leadership.

Fedorov had focused on tech-driven warfare and was credited with being part of the turnaround on the battlefield due to drone dominance. He was also popular with many Ukrainians for focusing on rooting out corruption. Thousands of Ukrainians protested his firing.

With the protests, Syrskyi was not chosen as defense minister, and no longer has his role as Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces (in Ukraine, that position reports to the defense minister).

Describing Fedorov, Budanov calls him, “a person without military experience. I’m not even speaking about the live combat experience, I’m speaking about just the experience in the military, a person without such experience cannot be in charge of the military ministry.” 

Fedorov’s replacement is Yevhenii Khmara, who has combat experience. Mykhailo Drapatyi is the new commander of the armed forces. Budanov says time will tell whether they’ll be effective butNA calls on Ukrainians to give them the chance.

Regarding the corruption Fedorov was after, Budanov says, “All the politicians are campaigning and getting positions using slogans of fighting corruption.”

He explained it is the minister’s responsibility to eradicate corruption. The general also points out there are anti-corruption organizations to help. 

Budanov’s name has come up in an investigation by NABU, one of the anti-corruption organizations. He did not seem concerned, however.

“I’ve always had very deep respect for our National Anti-Corruption Bureau and Special Anti-Corruption Prosecution,” he said in the interview. “That’s why I’m convinced that they will find out the smallest details who’s to blame and what are the mistakes or what are the felonies that they have committed.”

Persevering despite the war

A Ukrainian flag waves during the flag-raising ceremony to mark the National Flag Day at the WWII memorial in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Aug. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)

Despite the war, life goes on. When asked what music he listens to on good days and bad, he laughed and listed hard rock, heavy metal (including Metallica) and some classical. His religion, family and specifically his wife help keep him grounded and bring him joy.

“She always supports me and when she’s nearby I’m not afraid of anything,” he told NewsNation.

That laughter, though, seems rare, which is not surprising since Ukraine is fighting for its survival. Throughout the interview, Budanov referenced the importance of “human capital,” including the soldiers and civilians.

“Capital is something you need to take care of, try not to lose at least and try to increase at most,” the general continued.

His message to Trump and Ukrainian soldiers? Believe in Ukraine.

data.title: Trump '99 percent certain' he could have spoken at 9/11 event in New York City 'if I wanted to'
data.description:
President Trump said Friday that he’s “99 percent” sure he could have given a speech at the New York City 9/11 ceremony if he wanted to, while pushing back on reports that said he didn’t attend because he wouldn’t be able to give a speech.

“It’s just not true. I didn’t demand to speak,” he told Sid Rosenberg on 77 WABC Friday.

“I’m sure if I wanted to speak, they would have let me,” he said, adding that he’s president and he knows “the guys down there.”

“I am 99 percent sure,” he continued.

The New York Times reported last month that the president’s team told the organizers of New York’s ceremony that he would like to speak. The National September 11 Memorial and Museum has banned speeches from politicians at the ceremony since 2012.

Trump joked that “I speak enough, the last thing I want to do is speak.”

“I don’t need it for any reason,” he said.

He singled out New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman, who was one of the reporters behind the report. The president railed against the report in a Truth Social post last month, calling it “Corrupt News.”

“I’ve been to New York many times over the years, and no one ever speaks, it’s a ‘solemn ceremony!’” he wrote.

Trump instead attended and gave remarks at the 9/11 ceremony at the Pentagon, while Vice President Vance attended the New York memorial service.

Some presidents in the past visited all three sites — New York City, Arlington, Virginia for the Pentagon, and Shanksville, Pennsylvania for United Airlines Flight 93 — including former President Biden in 2021 for the 20th anniversary, former President Obama in 2011 for the 10th anniversary and former President George W. Bush on the first and fifth anniversaries.

data.title: Cruz on $5K dividend: 'I don't think we should be paying people that are not working'
data.description:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), a prominent conservative voice in the Senate GOP conference, says he’s willing to support President Trump’s proposal to give $5,000 dividend payments to U.S. adults provided that they are structured as tax refunds and go to people who work and pay taxes.

Asked about Trump’s proposal, Cruz told Fox News’ Jesse Watters that his support “depends on how it’s structured.”

“I would like to see it structured as a tax refund,” he said. “I would be all for structuring it as a tax refund.

“But I think we should be incentivizing work. I don’t think we should be paying people that are not working,” he argued.

Trump unveiled the proposal at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas and has drawn pushback from both Republican moderates and conservatives.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) warned the idea would be “extraordinarily costly.”

“From the few details we have, it seems that the proposed $5,000 dividend would not have an income cap and would be extraordinarily costly,” she said in a statement.

Paying out a $5,000 dividend to nearly 270 million American adults would cost more than $1 trillion and add to the national debt that recently passed the $40 trillion mark.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has defended the idea of putting money back in Americans’ pockets but he hasn’t committed to voting on the proposal on the Senate floor.

Asked during a recent Fox News interview whether Senate Republicans would pass Trump’s proposal, Thune replied: “Well, that’s a good question.”

“We’ll cross that bridge when we come to it,” he said.

data.title: House to take up Russia sanctions bill next week
data.description:
The House is set to take up legislation next week aimed at imposing tougher sanctions on Russia, after the measure cleared the Senate with overwhelming bipartisan support last month.

The House Rules Committee will meet Monday to consider the Russia sanctions bill, championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and backed by President Trump, along with other legislation. House GOP leaders are seeking to move the measure through regular order, meaning Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) will need near-unanimous Republican support on a procedural vote to advance the bill on the floor.

It remains unclear whether Johnson has enough GOP votes to clear that hurdle, setting up a potential test for House Republicans before the chamber can take up the underlying legislation for final passage.

The measure could also face resistance from Democrats, who have bristled at giving Trump tariff authorities even if they want to find a way to provide additional U.S. support to Ukraine. They argue that the president already has ample authority to impose sanctions on companies, individuals and oil tankers financing Russia’s war machine. 

Johnson told The Washington Examiner earlier this week at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas that “there should be bipartisan consensus” around the bill. 

Margus Tsahkna, the minister of foreign affairs of the Republic of Estonia, wrote on the social platform X that, “Estonia strongly supports imposing additional sanctions on Russia. We commend the U.S. Congress for their efforts and hope to see the Russian sanctions bill pass into law.”

If enacted, the measure would impose harsher sanctions on Russia and buyers of Russian oil and gas than the U.S. has previously enforced and extend existing sanctions on Iran, aiming to economically squeeze the two countries. The bill passed the Senate with broad bipartisan support last month.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), the lead Democratic sponsor of the measure, hailed it as a huge victory, and recalled some of the final words he heard from Graham, the chief GOP sponsor, about the bill’s imminent passage.

“As he said to me in some of his last words, this is a big f’ing deal. We all did good,” he said. “A bipartisan team achieved this overwhelming 86-11 vote. President Zelensky is watching in Ukraine. President Putin is watching in Moscow.”

data.title: Wall Street Journal editorial board denounces 'preposterous' Trump dividend plan
data.description:
The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board on Thursday slammed President Trump’s proposal to dole out $5,000 checks to every U.S. adult if the GOP wins control in both houses of Congress this November. 

The board noted in its opinion that this plan would amount to about $1.2 trillion when applied to the country’s roughly 240 million adult citizens. 

“The amount is so preposterous that you’d almost think Mr. Trump is trying to show voters the absurdity of such income redistribution,” the board wrote. 

The president debuted this controversial plan during his speech at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) convention in Dallas Wednesday evening. He has not clarified where this money would be sourced. 

“Here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them … because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump told the crowd. 

The proposal drew immediate backlash, including from some Republicans. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) warned its implementation could “lead to more debt and inflation,” while former GOP Rep. Bob Good (Va.) knocked it as a “socialist vote-buying scheme.”

The outlet’s editorial board accused the president of using this proposal to distract from discontent within the Republican Party around his administration’s tariffs on U.S. trade partners like Canada and Mexico. 

“Mr. Trump is resorting to this because voters are unhappy about inflation and don’t think his economic policies have helped them,” the board members wrote. “His tariff tax increases are a big part of the reason. If he repealed those, he’d give the country an economic dividend without spending a dime.”

The U.S. imposed tariffs last month on a large swath of Canadian goods after the two countries failed to reach a new trade agreement. After Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs, Trump announced heightened tariffs on Canadian imports to go into effect early next year. 

The president’s economic approval rating has also taken a hit during his administration’s ongoing military operations against Iran. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil trading corridor, has driven up global energy rates. 

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

data.title: 9/11 widow calls out government for protecting Saudis at 9/11 ceremony
data.description:
Terry Strada, the widow of a 9/11 victim, called on the Trump administration Friday to recognize Saudi Arabia’s alleged ties to this terrorist attack — an accusation that the kingdom has repeatedly denied. 

Strada’s comments at the 25th anniversary memorial service at Ground Zero in New York City elicited loud applause from the crowd. All former living U.S. presidents and Vice President Vance were in attendance. 

“For 25 years, administration after administration, including leaders in front of us today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families,” she said. 

“They withheld evidence,” Strada continued. “They vetoed [the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act]. They broke promises, both public and private. It was but one betrayal after another.”

Strada’s husband, bond broker Tom Strada, was killed in the North Tower of the World Trade Center during the 2001 attacks.

The widow, who chairs the advocacy organization, 9/11 Families United, called on President Trump to “tell the Saudis to stop lying.”

“Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through,” Strada said. 

She thanked Vance for attending the event and urged him to “carry that message back” to the president, who spoke at a 9/11 memorial service at the Pentagon on Friday. 

“Stand with the families. Stand with the survivors. Stand with Americans,” Strada said. “As my husband Tom would have said, that is always the right thing to do.”

A man who identified himself as the nephew of 9/11 victim Lisa Marie Terry called on the president to make documents public that he alleged would prove the country’s ties to these attacks.

“For 25 years, the deep state has hidden the truth about what happened that day 25 years ago,” he said. “President Trump, you’re our last hope. Release the unredacted files that implicate Saudi Arabia while what’s left of the victims’ families are still alive to see it.”

Both comments were made during the ceremony’s annual reading of the names of those killed during the terrorist attacks. Political speeches are traditionally not a part of this service. 

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment. 

The American president’s relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his two terms in the White House have drawn public scrutiny. Trump has brushed aside U.S. intelligence reports that found the ruler likely ordered the 2018 killing of Washington Post reporter Jamal Khashoggi.
